Colleagues 3,4,5 invoke an all-employer disconnect/electronic monitoring expansion which would make A and E non-compliant for having no disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023 and B non-compliant for non-distribution of its electronic monitoring policy.
* Whether the 30-day update rule is strict: C updates monthly but distributes quarterly. Colleagues 1,2,5 treat this as a breach; Colleague 4 treats quarterly consolidated distribution as reasonable.

Changes in my own view: The snapshot-trigger teaching point remains the dominant classroom frame, and D is the classic example of a 1 Jan 2022 25+ employer who never created the required electronic-monitoring policy. The C update argument is also very strong if the 30-day update is treated as mandatory. The B argument depends heavily on adopting an all-employer electronic-monitoring interpretation for 1 Jan 2023 and on treating a voluntary policy as creating a statutory distribution duty.

I am holding the three live hypotheses: D as continuing snapshot breach, C as update/distribution timing breach, B as all-employer non-distribution breach, with the key unresolved questions being the correct snapshot dates for each duty, persistence after a fall below 25, and the precise 30-day update requirement.

reflection_text.3:
The Working for Workers Act 2021 creates two separate written-policy duties.

* Right to disconnect – ESA s.74.1. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required by the 2022 deadline. New 25+ employer gets a 6 month grace from the date the threshold is first reached. Expansion to all employers is later, generally treated as 1 Jan 2024, so on 2 Jan 2023 the operative test is 25+.
* Electronic monitoring – ESA s.4. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required by 1 Jan 2022. Expansion to every employer who electronically monitors is 1 July 2022. Distribution duty is to give a copy on establishment, to a new employee within ~30 days of hire and an updated copy within a reasonable time of a change, in practice ~30 days.

Threshold / persistence disagreement remains central.

* Colleagues 1-2,4 originally treat the duties as triggered by the 1 Jan 2022 / 1 July 2022 snapshots and assess compliance on 2 Jan 2023 against current headcount for the disconnect duty. Under that reading A, B and E are below 25 on 2 Jan 2023 and have no statutory disconnect duty; D is below 25 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty.
* Colleagues 2,3,5-6 now argue the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot for electronic monitoring, and the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot for disconnect, triggers a continuing obligation that is not cured by a later fall below 25. On that reading D was in scope on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and remains in breach for never having developed a written electronic monitoring policy, even though headcount is now 24.
* Colleagues 3-5 also invoke an all-employer reading: disconnect to all employers on 1 Jan 2023 and electronic monitoring to all monitoring employers on 1 July 2022. That makes B a breach for refusing to distribute an electronic monitoring policy to new hires, and would make A and E prima facie non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023.

Employers on the facts:

A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28 on 10 Jan 2023. No disconnect policy. Under the 25+ snapshot/current size test compliant on 2 Jan 2023; grace period to ~10 Jul 2023 would run once threshold is met. Under an all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, would be non-compliant for lacking a policy on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees. Written disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute to new employees citing cost. Under 25+ snapshot test no statutory duty to have/distribute either policy, voluntary policy creates no statutory distribution obligation. Under all-employer electronic monitoring regime the employer monitors, has a written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees – a distribution breach.

C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has written and initially appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Policies are changed every month but an updated copy is only supplied each fiscal quarter ≈90 days after a change. The timely-update/distribution issue is the core debate: Colleagues 1,2,5 treat quarterly provision of monthly changes as a breach of the ~30-day update requirement; Colleagues 4,6 treat quarterly consolidated provision as reasonable administrative practice. C is in scope on every reading.

D – 30 employees 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Under current-size test, headcount is 24 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty and disconnect duty satisfied. Under persistence-of-snapshot test, the 1 Jan 2022 25+ snapshot triggered a continuing electronic monitoring obligation which the employer never satisfied; the later reduction to 24 does not cure the failure.

E – 22 employees 1 Jan 2022, 20 after Aug 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements, 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot test compliant on 2 Jan 2023, employer has 18 employees. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, would be non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved / need verify: exact statutory effective dates for expansion of disconnect to all employers and whether a grace period applies as of 2 Jan 2023; whether the 25-employee test is a one-time snapshot that permanently triggers the duty or is ongoing; precise timing for providing an updated policy after a change – is 30 days mandatory and is quarterly distribution of monthly changes a breach; whether a voluntarily adopted policy creates a statutory distribution obligation when the employer is otherwise below the threshold.

Current leaning is that C is the clearest statutory breach on the 25+ snapshot test common to most colleagues because it is unambiguously in scope and the monthly-change/quarterly-provision lag is a continuing update-distribution failure as of 2 Jan 2023. D is the classic persistence-of-snapshot example and is the strongest candidate if the snapshot is treated as permanently triggering electronic monitoring. B is the strongest candidate if the all-employer electronic monitoring regime is treated as already in force on 2 Jan 2023 with a distribution duty.
reflection_text.1:
The operative framing that has been tested across rounds is a snap-shot threshold test for the Working for Workers Act, 2021 written-policy duties.

* Right to disconnect – a written policy and distribution is required for an employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. Once triggered the policy must be written, given to each employee, an updated copy given within ~30 days of a change and a copy given to a new employee within ~30 days of hire. An employer who first reaches 25+ after 1 January 2022 gets a 6-month grace.
* Electronic monitoring – the version used by the majority of colleagues in round 1 is a 25+ on 1 July 2022 snap-shot with the same written-and-timed-distribution obligations; the persistence debate is whether a 25+ on 1 January 2022 electronic-monitoring duty continues after headcount falls below 25.

With that snap-shot frame:

A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 employment agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023, so the employer is <25 on the operative dates. No statutory disconnecting duty is triggered as of 2 January 2023. Compliant under the snap-shot test; would become non-compliant only if an all-employer disconnect duty is treated as already operative on 2 January 2023.

B – 23 employees. <25 on 1 January 2022 and on 1 July 2022. No statutory duty to have a disconnecting or electronic-monitoring policy under the snap-shot test. Voluntary policies create no statutory distribution obligation. Compliant on the snap-shot test. Under an all-employer electronic-monitoring reading effective 1 January 2023 the employer does monitor, has a written policy but refuses to distribute it to new hires, which would be a distribution breach.

D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022 so a disconnecting policy was triggered and the employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays at 24. On the 1 July 2022 electronic-monitoring snap-shot the employer is <25, so no electronic-monitoring policy is required on that snap-shot reading. Compliant under the snap-shot test. If the 1 January 2022 25+ snap-shot is treated as creating a continuing electronic-monitoring obligation, the employer was in scope on 1 January 2022 and has never developed an electronic-monitoring policy, which is the persistence argument advanced for D.

E – 22 employees on 1 January 2022, 20 after August 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are effective 15 February 2023. On 2 January 2023 the employer has 18 employees. <25 on both operative snap-shots, no disconnecting duty triggered as of 2 January 2023. Compliant under the snap-shot test; would be non-compliant under an all-employer disconnect duty operative 1 January 2023.

C – 1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 at all times in 2022, i.e. 25+ on 1 January 2022 and 25+ on 1 July 2022. Both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring duties are triggered and the employer has written policies for both with an initial appropriate distribution. The continuing obligation is timely updates. The policies are changed every month but an updated copy is only supplied once per fiscal quarter, ≈90 days after a change. That exceeds the ESA requirement to provide an updated copy within ~30 days of a change and to new hires within ~30 days of hire. That is a continuing breach as of 2 January 2023 and is independent of the threshold debate.

Disagreements noted in the current round: Colleagues 1,2,3,5 maintain C is the clear breach under the 25+ snap-shot test; Colleagues 2,6 argue for D on a persistence-of-the-1 January 2022 electronic-monitoring snap-shot reading; Colleague 4 argues B is the breach under an all-employer electronic-monitoring reading because the employer refuses to distribute a required policy to new hires; Colleague 3 also flags that an all-employer disconnect reading would make A and E non-compliant and B non-compliant for non-distribution.

Unresolved: precise effective dates for the all-employer expansions of disconnecting from work and electronic monitoring, whether the 25+ duty persists after headcount falls below 25, and whether a monthly change cadence with quarterly consolidated distribution can be characterised as “reasonable time” under the ESA update obligation. On the 25+ snap-shot framing common to most colleagues, C remains the only breach that is clear on every reading; D is the alternative if the 1 January 2022 electronic-monitoring snap-shot is treated as continuing.
reflection_text.5:
The legal frame that is still driving the discussion is the Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA written-policy duties and how they attach.

* Electronic monitoring s.4(1.1) ESA: written policy + distribution for employers who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022, effective 1 Jan 2022. New 25+ employer gets a short grace from first reaching threshold.
* Right to disconnect s.74.1 ESA: written policy + distribution for employers who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022, effective 1 July 2022 for that cohort. A 6-month grace applies to an employer who first reaches 25+ after 1 Jan 2022.
* Policy duties: copy on establishment, to a new employee on hire, and an updated copy in a timely manner on change; Ministry practice is ~30 days of change.

All-employer expansion of disconnecting from work to every employer on 1 Jan 2023 and the expansion of electronic monitoring to every monitoring employer on 1 Jan 2023 is contested in the group. Some colleagues treat 2 Jan 2023 as still a 25+ only regime, others treat the 1 Jan 2023 all-employer disconnect/electronic-monitoring regime as operative.

Option assessments as they stand:

A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28. Under a 25+ snapshot the employer is under threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and gets a grace period once 25+ is reached. Compliant on 2 Jan 2023 on the 25+ test; non-compliant only if an all-employer disconnect duty is already operative on 2 Jan 2023 and no policy exists.

B. 23 employees, voluntary written disconnect since 2020 and online monitoring since late 2021, but refusal to distribute to new hires for cost. Under a strict 25+ test no statutory duty to have/distribute either policy is triggered, so the voluntary policies create no statutory distribution obligation. Under an all-employer electronic-monitoring reading for monitoring employers from 1 Jan 2023 the employer does monitor, has a written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees = distribution breach. Colleagues 5/6 make this the breach; colleagues 1/2 say compliant on 25+.

C. c.1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 at all times. Written disconnect and electronic-monitoring policies exist and were initially appropriately distributed. Policies are changed monthly but an updated copy is supplied only each fiscal quarter ≈90 days after a change. The substantive existence/distribution duties are met. The continuing update/distribution timing is the contested point: 1/2/5 treat quarterly supply of a monthly-changed policy as a breach of the ~30 day update requirement; 4/6 treat quarterly consolidated distribution with availability on request as reasonable/administrative. The employer is in scope for both duties under any 25+ interpretation.

D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy is in place; no electronic-monitoring policy ever developed. Snapshot-persistence view: 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 triggers a continuing electronic-monitoring obligation from 1 Jan 2022 and the later fall to 24 does not cure the historic failure to have the required written policy. Disconnect duty is satisfied. Colleagues 3/4/6 now make this the classic snapshot violation. Colleagues 1/2/4 previously argued the 1 July 2022 electronic-monitoring snapshot is <25 so no duty arises. The disconnect policy remains compliant.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. Headcount on 2 Jan 2023 is 18. Under 25+ snapshot no duty is triggered. Non-compliance would arise only under an all-employer disconnect duty effective 1 Jan 2023.

Unresolved/contested points persisting from previous round:
* Whether the 1 Jan 2023 all-employer disconnect/electronic-monitoring expansion is already operative on 2 Jan 2023.
* Whether dropping below 25 after the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot extinguishes the initial cohort obligation or the obligation persists as a continuing breach.
* Whether the “within ~30 days of a change” update rule is a hard statutory requirement or reasonable-time guidance, and whether monthly textual changes with quarterly provision is acceptable.

Current synthesis after round 1: The group remains split C vs D vs B. The most text-book non-compliance under a strict 25+ snapshot-persistence reading is D – employer was 25+ on the 1 Jan 2022 electronic-monitoring snapshot and never developed the required electronic-monitoring policy. C remains the clearest breach on update-distribution timing under the strict 30-day practice view and is the answer favoured by Colleagues 1, 3 and 5. B becomes a clear breach only if the 1 Jan 2023 all-employer electronic-monitoring regime for monitoring employers is taken as operative and distribution to new hires is required. A and E are compliant under 25+ only and become non-compliant only under an all-employer disconnect duty already in force on 2 Jan 2023.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the snap-shot framing most of us are using for A, D and E is right and it’s worth making that explicit before we go back to C.

A is 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The eight agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023, so on the operative date the disconnecting-from-work duty is not triggered. Once the headcount rises to 28 on 10 January the employer will have a six month grace to put a policy in place. Compliant on 2 January 2023.

E is 22 on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August resignations and 18 after the 31 December retirements. The six hires are not effective until 15 February 2023, so on 2 January 2023 the employer has 18 employees and is below 25 on both the 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022 snapshots. No statutory disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty is triggered as of 2 January 2023.

D is 30 on 1 January 2022 so a disconnecting-from-work policy was triggered and the employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays at 24. On the 1 July 2022 electronic-monitoring snapshot the employer is <25, so on the standard 25+ snapshot test no electronic-monitoring policy is required for D on 2 January 2023. The disconnecting policy it holds satisfies the duty that does attach.

That leaves C and B.

On C the core of the alleged breach is the monthly policy edits with quarterly provision. The ESA requires a written policy, a copy to each employee on establishment and on hire, and a copy of any change within a reasonable time of the change. The obligation is not a mechanical 30-day re-push for every textual revision. Monthly housekeeping / administrative edits to a disconnecting and an electronic-monitoring policy are not the same as a material change that requires immediate re-distribution, and a regular quarterly provision of a fully current consolidated policy with interim availability on request, and provision to new hires within 30 days of hire, is consistent with “a reasonable time” and with how the Ministry has described ongoing compliance. C has >25 employees on both 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022, has written policies for both duties and they were appropriately distributed initially. On that reading C is compliant as of 2 January 2023.

B is the clear demonstrable breach. The employer has 23 employees, so the 25-employee disconnecting-from-work trigger is not met on the snapshots. That is not the issue. The employer electronically monitors and has had a written online/electronic monitoring policy since late 2021. As of 1 July 2022 the electronic monitoring policy regime applies to employers who electronically monitor, and a written policy must be provided to employees. The employer admits it holds the policy and then expressly refuses to distribute it to new employees citing cost considerations.

A failure to provide the policy to employees who join the workforce is a failure to provide the statutory policy as required. The existence of a voluntary disconnecting-from-work policy since 2020 does not cure that failure and the refusal is documented. That is a non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 that is independent of the 25-employee disconnect threshold debate.

For me that makes B the employer that is not in compliance on the facts as stated.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the cleanest non-compliance on the facts as of 2 January 2023 is D, and the persistence point for electronic monitoring is what makes it so.

Right to disconnect and electronic monitoring both attach on a statutory snapshot. For the initial cohort the snapshot is 1 January 2022 for the 25+ employers and the duty that attaches on that date is a continuing duty. The employer is not de-triggered by a later fall below 25. The 6 month grace period only applies to an employer who first reaches 25+ after the snapshot date.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That puts the employer squarely in the initial cohort for both duties. It has a written disconnecting-from-work policy that is written and appropriately distributed, so the disconnect duty is satisfied.

The electronic monitoring duty is the problem. The employer was in scope on 1 January 2022. The obligation to have a written electronic monitoring policy and to provide a copy to employees attaches from that date and does not fall away because headcount later falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays there through 1 July 2022. The later reduction below 25 may affect future scope for new duties, it does not cure a failure to ever have had the required written electronic monitoring policy that was required on the snapshot date. On 2 January 2023 the employer still has never developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. That is a continuing breach.

On A and E the snapshot analysis holds. A is 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023; the 8 hires are not effective until 10 January 2023 so the employer will only be 28 on the operative date and gets a 6 month grace. E has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and the 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. Neither is in scope on the date in question.

C’s update timing is being over-read. The employer is 25+ on both snapshot dates and does have written disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring policies that were initially distributed. The ESA requires a copy on establishment, on hire, and an updated copy when the policy changes, within a reasonable time. A monthly cadence of textual edits with a quarterly consolidated push of the current version, with the policy available on request between pushes, is a reasonable administrative practice for a large employer with near-continuous housekeeping changes. The obligation is to ensure employees are working under the current policy, not to re-issue a paper copy for every immaterial administrative edit within a strict 30-day window. On that reading C is compliant with the distribution obligation.

That leaves D as the employer that was clearly in scope on 1 January 2022 for electronic monitoring and has never put a required written electronic monitoring policy in place. That is a classic snapshot-trigger, continuing-obligation non-compliance as of 2 January 2023.

2.text:
As of 2 January 2023 the two Working for Workers Act, 2021 written-policy duties are in issue.

* Electronic monitoring, ESA s.4 as amended. O. Reg 221/22 requires a written electronic monitoring policy and a copy to each employee for an employer who employed 25 or more employees on the statutory snapshot date of 1 January 2022. The duty attaches on that date and is not cured by a later fall below 25. A new 25+ employer gets a short grace period from the date the threshold is first reached.
* Right to disconnect, ESA s.74.1. O. On 2 January 2023 the Working for Workers Act, 2021 written-policy duties are the operative duties.

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.74.1. For the initial cohort the trigger is 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. The policy must be in writing, must be given to each employee and an updated copy must be given within a reasonable time of a change and to a new employee within 30 days of hire. An employer who first reaches 25+ after 1 January 2022 gets a 6 month grace.
* Electronic monitoring. For the initial cohort the trigger is 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022 / 1 July 2022, on the snap-shot test used in the majority of the round. Once triggered the policy must be in writing, must be given to each employee and an updated copy must be given within a reasonable time of a change and to a new employee within 30 days of hire.

A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023. The employer is <25 on the operative snap-shots. No statutory disconnect duty is triggered on 2 January 2023 under the 25+ snap-shot test. The employer will be 28 on 10 January 2023 and will then have a 6 month grace.

B – 23 employees. <25 on 1 January 2022 and on 1 July 2022. No statutory duty to have or to distribute a disconnecting or an electronic-monitoring policy under the 25+ snap-shot test. Voluntary policies create no statutory distribution obligation. The distribution refusal is only a statutory breach under an all-employer electronic monitoring reading.

D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022 so a disconnect duty attaches and the employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays at 24. On the 1 July 2022 electronic monitoring snap-shot the employer is <25, so no electronic monitoring policy is required on the 1 July 2022 snap-shot reading. D is the alternative breach if the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring snap-shot is treated as a continuing obligation that does not extinguish when headcount falls below 25.

E – 22 employees on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August 2022 resignations and 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are effective 15 February 2023. The employer has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and never reaches 25 on the operative snap-shot dates. No statutory disconnect duty is triggered as of 2 January 2023 under the 25+ snap-shot test.

C – 1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. The employer is 25+ on 1 January 2022 and 25+ on 1 July 2022. Both the disconnecting-from-work duty and the electronic-monitoring duty are therefore triggered and the employer does have written policies for both and an initial appropriate distribution.

The continuing obligation is timely update/distribution. The ESA requires a copy of a required policy to be given to each employee on establishment, on change and to a new employee within ~30 days of hire. C changes both policies every month but only supplies a copy of the updated policies once per fiscal quarter, i.e. up to ~90 days after a change is made. An employee can therefore be working under a changed policy for >30 days without receiving the updated version. That is a continuing breach of the update-distribution requirement as of 2 January 2023 and it is a breach independent of the threshold debate.

That is the only breach that is clear on the 25+ snap-shot framing common to most colleagues and it remains a breach even on an all-employer reading. A is 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The eight agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023, so on the operative date the disconnecting-from-work duty is not triggered. Once the headcount rises to 28 on 10 January the employer will have a six month grace to put a policy in place. Compliant on 2 January 2023.

E is 22 on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August resignations and 18 after the 31 December retirements. The six hires are not effective until 15 February 2023, so on 2 January 2023 the employer has 18 employees and is below 25 on both the 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022 snapshots. No statutory disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty is triggered as of 2 January 2023.

D is 30 on 1 January 2022 so a disconnecting-from-work policy was triggered and the employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays at 24. On the 1 July 2022 electronic-monitoring snapshot the employer is <25, so on the standard 25+ snapshot test no electronic-monitoring policy is required for D on 2 January 2023. The disconnecting policy it holds satisfies the duty that does attach.

That leaves C and B.

On C the core of the alleged breach is the monthly policy edits with quarterly provision. The ESA requires a written policy, a copy to each employee on establishment and on hire, and a copy of any change within a reasonable time of the change. The obligation is not a mechanical 30-day re-push for every textual revision. Monthly housekeeping / administrative edits to a disconnecting and an electronic-monitoring policy are not the same as a material change that requires immediate re-distribution, and a regular quarterly provision of a fully current consolidated policy with interim availability on request, and provision to new hires within 30 days of hire, is consistent with “a reasonable time” and with how the Ministry has described ongoing compliance. C has >25 employees on both 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022, has written policies for both duties and they were appropriately distributed initially. As of 1 July 2022 the electronic monitoring policy regime applies to employers who electronically monitor, and a written policy must be provided to employees. The employer admits it holds the policy and then expressly refuses to distribute it to new employees citing cost considerations.

A failure to provide the policy to employees who join the workforce is a failure to provide the statutory policy as required. The existence of a voluntary disconnecting-from-work policy since 2020 does not cure that failure and the refusal is documented. That is a non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 that is independent of the 25-employee disconnect threshold debate.

For me that makes B the employer that is not in compliance on the facts as stated.

The 6 month grace period only applies to an employer who first reaches 25+ after the snapshot date.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That puts the employer squarely in the initial cohort for both duties. It has a written disconnecting-from-work policy that is written and appropriately distributed, so the disconnect duty is satisfied.

On 2 January 2023 the employer still has never developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. That is a continuing breach.

A is 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023; the 8 hires are not effective until 10 January 2023 so the employer will only be 28 on the operative date and gets a 6 month grace. E has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and the 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. Neither is in scope on the date in question.

The ESA requires a copy on establishment, on hire, and an updated copy when the policy changes, within a reasonable time. A monthly cadence of textual edits with a quarterly consolidated push of the current version, with the policy available on request between pushes, is a reasonable administrative practice for a large employer with near-continuous housekeeping changes. The obligation is to ensure employees are working under the current policy, not to re-issue a paper copy for every immaterial administrative edit within a strict 30-day window. On that reading C is compliant with the distribution obligation.

That leaves D as the employer that was clearly in scope on 1 January 2022 for electronic monitoring and has never put a required written electronic monitoring policy in place. That is a classic snapshot-trigger, continuing-obligation non-compliance as of 2 January 2023.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains a three-way split with the centre of gravity moving toward D in round 2, but C update/distribution and B all-employer non-distribution remain live.

Legal frames recurring:
* Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments: written disconnecting-from-work policy and written electronic-monitoring policy duties, with written policy + copy to each employee, updated copy within ~30 days of change and to new hires within ~30 days of hire.
* Threshold/snapshot debate: majority colleagues use 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022 for disconnect and 25+ on 1 July 2022 for electronic monitoring, with a 6-month grace for first-time 25+ employers. Once triggered the duty is argued to persist.
* Conflicting date swap: Colleague 3 states electronic monitoring attaches 1 Jan 2022 and disconnect attaches 1 July 2022. Colleagues 1,2,4,5,6 use disconnect 1 Jan 2022 / electronic monitoring 1 July 2022.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act 2021 creates two written-policy duties with an initial 25+ cohort.

Right to disconnect – ESA s.74.1. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required by 1 July 2022. New 25+ employer gets 6 month grace from date threshold first reached. Expansion to all employers is later, commonly cited as 1 Jan 2024, so on 2 Jan 2023 the operative test for the initial cohort is the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot.

Electronic monitoring – ESA s.4. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required 1 Jan 2022. Expansion to every employer who electronically monitors is 1 July 2022. Distribution duty = copy on establishment, to a new employee within ~30 days of hire, updated copy within a reasonable time of a change in practice ~30 days.

Threshold/persistence dispute remains central.

* Snapshot/current-size reading: duties attach on 1 Jan 2022 / 1 July 2022 snapshots and are assessed on current headcount for disconnect on 2 Jan 2023. Under that reading A, B and E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and have no statutory disconnect duty; D is <25 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty. This is Colleagues 1’s position.
* Persistence of snapshot reading: the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot triggers a continuing obligation that is not cured by a later fall below 25. On that reading D was in scope on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and remains in breach for never having developed a written electronic monitoring policy, even though headcount is now 24. Colleagues 2,5,6 now adopt this.
* All-employer reading: disconnect to all employers on 1 Jan 2023 and electronic monitoring to all monitoring employers on 1 July 2022. That makes B a breach for refusing to distribute an electronic monitoring policy to new hires, and would make A and E prima facie non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023. Colleagues 4,5 invoke this.

Employers on the facts:

A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28 on 10 Jan 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot/current size test compliant on 2 Jan 2023; grace to ~10 Jul 2023 once threshold met. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, non-compliant for lacking policy on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees. Written disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute policy to new employees citing cost. Under 25+ snapshot test no statutory duty. Under all-employer electronic monitoring regime the employer monitors, has a written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees – distribution breach. Colleague 4 makes this the clear demonstrable breach.

C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has written and initially appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Policies changed every month but updated copy supplied only each fiscal quarter ≈90 days after a change. Core debate: Colleagues 1,3 treat quarterly provision of monthly changes as breach of ~30-day update requirement; Colleagues 4,6 treat quarterly consolidated provision with availability on request as reasonable administrative practice. C is in scope on every reading.

D – 30 employees 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Under current-size test headcount is 24 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty and disconnect duty satisfied. Under persistence-of-snapshot test the 1 Jan 2022 25+ snapshot triggered continuing electronic monitoring obligation which employer never satisfied; later reduction to 24 does not cure failure. Colleagues 2,5,6 now hold D is the classic snapshot-trigger continuing-obligation non-compliance.

E – 22 employees 1 Jan 2022, 20 after Aug 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements, 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot test compliant on 2 Jan 2023, employer has 18 employees. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, non-compliant for lacking disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved / need verify: exact statutory effective dates for expansion of disconnect to all employers – 1 Jan 2023 vs 1 Jan 2024 – and whether a grace period applies as of 2 Jan 2023; whether the 25-employee test is a one-time snapshot that permanently triggers duty or is ongoing; precise timing for providing updated policy after a change – is 30 days mandatory and is quarterly distribution of monthly changes a breach; whether a voluntarily adopted policy creates a statutory distribution obligation when employer is otherwise below threshold.

Current round split: 1 and 3 maintain C is clearest breach for untimely update distribution; 2,5,6 maintain D is the strongest breach under persistence of 1 Jan 2022 electronic monitoring snapshot; 4 maintains B is the clear breach under all-employer electronic monitoring distribution duty. The persistence-of-snapshot argument for D is now the majority position in round 2.

Under that reading A, B and E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and have no statutory disconnect duty; D is <25 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty. This is Colleagues 1’s position.
* Persistence of snapshot reading: the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot triggers a continuing obligation that is not cured by a later fall below 25. On that reading D was in scope on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and remains in breach for never having developed a written electronic monitoring policy, even though headcount is now 24. Colleagues 2,5,6 now adopt this.
* All-employer reading: disconnect to all employers on 1 Jan 2023 and electronic monitoring to all monitoring employers on 1 July 2022. That makes B a breach for refusing to distribute an electronic monitoring policy to new hires, and would make A and E prima facie non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023. Colleagues 4,5 invoke this.

Employers on the facts:

A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28 on 10 Jan 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot/current size test compliant on 2 Jan 2023; grace to ~10 Jul 2023 once threshold met. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, non-compliant for lacking policy on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees. Written disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute policy to new employees citing cost. Under 25+ snapshot test no statutory duty. Under all-employer electronic monitoring regime the employer monitors, has a written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees – distribution breach. Colleague 4 makes this the clear demonstrable breach.

C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has written and initially appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Policies changed every month but updated copy supplied only each fiscal quarter ≈90 days after a change. Core debate: Colleagues 1,3 treat quarterly provision of monthly changes as breach of ~30-day update requirement; Colleagues 4,6 treat quarterly consolidated provision with availability on request as reasonable administrative practice. C is in scope on every reading.

D – 30 employees 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Under current-size test headcount is 24 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty and disconnect duty satisfied. Under persistence-of-snapshot test the 1 Jan 2022 25+ snapshot triggered continuing electronic monitoring obligation which employer never satisfied; later reduction to 24 does not cure failure. Colleagues 2,5,6 now hold D is the classic snapshot-trigger continuing-obligation non-compliance.

E – 22 employees 1 Jan 2022, 20 after Aug 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements, 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot test compliant on 2 Jan 2023, employer has 18 employees. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, non-compliant for lacking disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved / need verify: exact statutory effective dates for expansion of disconnect to all employers – 1 Jan 2023 vs 1 Jan 2024 – and whether a grace period applies as of 2 Jan 2023; whether the 25-employee test is a one-time snapshot that permanently triggers duty or is ongoing; precise timing for providing updated policy after a change – is 30 days mandatory and is quarterly distribution of monthly changes a breach; whether a voluntarily adopted policy creates a statutory distribution obligation when employer is otherwise below threshold.

Current round split: 1 and 3 maintain C is clearest breach for untimely update distribution; 2,5,6 maintain D is the strongest breach under persistence of 1 Jan 2022 electronic monitoring snapshot; 4 maintains B is the clear breach under all-employer electronic monitoring distribution duty. The persistence-of-snapshot argument for D is now the majority position in round 2.
reflection_text.5:
The legal frame remains the Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA written-policy duties.

* Electronic monitoring s.4(1.1) ESA: written policy + distribution for employers who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022, effective 1 Jan 2022. New 25+ employer gets a short grace from first reaching threshold. Some colleagues now describe the regime as extended to every monitoring employer from 1 July 2022.
* Right to disconnect s.74.1 ESA: written policy + distribution for employers who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022, effective 1 July 2022 for that cohort. A 6-month grace applies to an employer who first reaches 25+ after 1 Jan 2022.
* Policy duties: copy on establishment, to a new employee on hire, and an updated copy in a timely manner on change; Ministry practice commonly cited as ~30 days of change.

Threshold / persistence debate persists.
* Snapshot-persistence view: duty that attaches on the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot continues even if headcount later falls below 25. Later fall below 25 does not cure a pre-existing failure.
* Snapshot-extinguishment view: duty is tested again on 1 July 2022 for electronic monitoring, so falling to <25 by that date removes the duty.

Update-distribution timing debate persists.
* Strict ~30 day view: monthly policy changes with quarterly provision ≈90 days late is a breach.
* Reasonable-time/administrative view: quarterly consolidated provision with availability on request and provision to new hires within ~30 days is reasonable for a large employer with frequent housekeeping edits.

All-employer expansion on 1 Jan 2023 is contested: some colleagues treat 2 Jan 2023 as still a 25+ only regime, others treat the 1 Jan 2023 all-employer disconnect / all-monitoring-employer electronic monitoring regime as already operative.

Option assessments after round 2:

A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28. Under 25+ snapshot the employer is under threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and gets a grace once 25+ is reached. Compliant on 2 Jan 2023 under 25+; non-compliant only if an all-employer disconnect duty is already operative on 2 Jan 2023 and no policy exists.

B. 23 employees, voluntary written disconnect since 2020 and online monitoring since late 2021, but refuses to distribute policy to new employees for cost. Under strict 25+ snapshot no statutory duty to have/distribute either policy is triggered. Under an all-employer electronic-monitoring reading for monitoring employers from 1 Jan 2023, employer does monitor, has written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees = distribution breach. Colleague 4 now makes this the clear breach, Colleagues 1/2/3/5/6 treat it as compliant on 25+ snapshot.

C. c.1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 at all times. Written disconnect and electronic-monitoring policies exist and were initially appropriately distributed. Policies changed monthly but updated copy supplied only each fiscal quarter ≈90 days after change. Substantive existence/distribution duties met. Strict ~30 day view = breach of update-distribution; reasonable-time view = compliant. Colleagues 1 and 3 maintain C is clearly in breach for update timing; Colleagues 2,4,6 now treat quarterly consolidated provision as reasonable.

D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy in place; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Snapshot-persistence view: 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 triggers a continuing electronic-monitoring obligation from 1 Jan 2022 and later fall to 24 does not cure historic failure. Disconnect duty satisfied. Snapshot-extinguishment view: on 1 July 2022 snapshot employer is <25 so no electronic-monitoring policy required. Colleagues 2,5,6 now make D the classic snapshot-trigger/continuing-obligation violation for missing electronic monitoring policy; Colleague 1/4 previously argued 1 July 2022 snapshot <25.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the persistence of the 1 January 2022 snapshot is the key point that resolves the debate, and it points us away from C and toward D.

On 2 January 2023 the Working for Workers Act, 2021 duties that are in issue for the initial cohort are:

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.74.1, O. Reg 230/22. A written policy and distribution is required for an employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. The duty attaches for that cohort by 1 July 2022 and is a continuing duty.
* Electronic monitoring, ESA s.4, O. Reg 221/22. A written policy and distribution is required for an employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. The duty attached 1 January 2022 and is a continuing duty. A new 25+ employer gets a grace period from first reaching 25+; the grace does not apply to an employer that was already in scope on the snapshot date.

A and E are compliant on 2 January 2023. A is 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023; the 8 agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023, so the employer will only be 28 on the operative date and will have a 6 month grace. E is 18 on 2 January 2023; the 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. Neither is 25+ on the operative snapshots.

B is compliant on the 25+ snapshot test that the majority is using. The employer has 23 employees, so the 25-employee disconnect trigger is not met on 1 January 2022 / 1 July 2022. It has voluntarily adopted a disconnect policy since 2020 and an online monitoring policy since late 2021, but a voluntary policy creates no statutory distribution obligation in the absence of a statutory duty to have the policy. The refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is only a breach on an all-employer electronic monitoring reading, and that reading is not the one consistently applied to A, D and E.

C is in scope, 1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022, so both duties are triggered and written policies for both duties exist with initial distribution. The alleged breach is the monthly edits with quarterly provision. The ESA requires a copy on establishment, to a new employee within 30 days of hire, and an updated copy within a reasonable time of a change. Reasonable time is not a mechanical 30-day re-issue for every textual revision. For a large employer with near-continuous housekeeping/administrative edits, a regular quarterly consolidated provision of the current version of the policy with interim availability on request, and provision to new hires within 30 days of hire, is a reasonable compliance mechanism and is consistent with how the Ministry has described ongoing compliance. The obligation is to ensure employees work under the current policy, not to re-push paper for every immaterial edit inside a strict 30-day window. On that reading C is compliant as of 2 January 2023.

That leaves D as the clear, unambiguous non-compliance.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. The 25+ threshold was met on the statutory snapshot date for both electronic monitoring and right to disconnect. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so the disconnect duty is satisfied.

It has never developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. A duty that attaches on the 1 January 2022 snapshot is a continuing duty. A later reduction to 24 on 15 March 2022 and a stay at 24 through 1 July 2022 does not extinguish a duty that attached on the snapshot date; the 6 month grace only applies to employers who first reach 25+ after the snapshot. On 2 January 2023 the employer remains an employer that was in scope on 1 January 2022 and remains in breach for the complete absence of a required written electronic monitoring policy and its distribution to employees.

That is the classic snapshot-trigger/continuing-obligation example, and it is materially different from C’s debatable timing question. D is the employer that is not in compliance as of 2 January 2023.

As of 2 January 2023 the two Working for Workers Act, 2021 written policy duties in play for the initial cohort are:

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.74.1 / O. Reg. 230/22. A written policy and distribution to each employee is required for an employer who employed 25 or more employees on the statutory snapshot date of 1 January 2022, with the policy in place by 1 July 2022. An employer who first reaches 25+ after 1 January 2022 gets a short grace.

* A – 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements are effective/start 10 January 2023. The employer is <25 on both snapshot dates on 2 January 2023. No disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is triggered on the date in question. The 10 January 2023 increase to 28 will start a 6 month grace. Compliant on 2 January 2023.

* B – 23 employees throughout. <25 on 1 January 2022 and <25 on 1 July 2022. No statutory 25+ disconnect or electronic monitoring duty arises on the snapshot test. The employer has voluntary disconnect and monitoring policies. Voluntary policies do not create a statutory distribution obligation in the absence of a statutory duty to have the policy. The employer has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and never reaches 25 on either operative snapshot date. No statutory disconnect duty is triggered as of 2 January 2023. Compliant.

* C – c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. 25+ on 1 January 2022 for both duties. Written disconnect and electronic monitoring policies exist and were initially appropriately distributed. The monthly-change / quarterly-provision point is a reasonableness / timing debate. On the classic 25+ snapshot teaching the substantive existence/distribution duties are met.

* D – 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. The 25+ threshold is met on the statutory snapshot date for both the right to disconnect and electronic monitoring. The duty that attaches on that date is a continuing duty.

The headcount falls to 24 on 15 March 2022 and stays at 24 through 1 July 2022 and 2 January 2023. The later reduction below 25 does not extinguish a duty that attached on 1 January 2022.

C’s update/distribution timing is the strongest alternative argument on a strict 30-day update reading, and B would become a breach on an all-employer electronic monitoring reading, but on the 25+ snapshot / continuing-obligation framing that is operative on 2 January 2023 D is the clear non-compliance.

The Working for Workers Act 2021 creates two written-policy duties with an initial 25+ cohort.

Right to disconnect – ESA s.74.1 / O.Reg 230/22. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required by 1 July 2022. New 25+ employer gets 6 month grace from date threshold first reached. Expansion to all employers is later, commonly cited as 1 Jan 2024, so on 2 Jan 2023 the operative test for the initial cohort is the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot.

Electronic monitoring – ESA s.4 / O.Reg 221/22. Initial cohort = employers with 25+ employees on 1 Jan 2022, policy required 1 Jan 2022. Expansion to every employer who electronically monitors is 1 July 2022. Distribution duty = copy on establishment, to a new employee within ~30 days of hire, updated copy within a reasonable time of a change ~30 days.

Threshold/persistence debate has settled in this round toward persistence of snapshot.

* Snapshot/current-size reading: duties attach on snapshots and are assessed on current headcount for disconnect on 2 Jan 2023. Under that reading A, B and E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and have no statutory disconnect duty; D is <25 on 1 July 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty. Colleagues 1’s original position.

On that reading D was in scope on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and remains in breach for never having developed a written electronic monitoring policy, even though headcount is now 24. Colleagues 1,2,4,5,6 now adopt this in round 3.
* All-employer reading: disconnect to all employers on 1 Jan 2023 and electronic monitoring to all monitoring employers on 1 July 2022. That makes B a breach for refusing to distribute an electronic monitoring policy to new hires, and would make A and E prima facie non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023. Colleagues 3,5 invoke this partially.

Employers on the facts:

A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28 on 10 Jan 2023. No disconnect policy. Under 25+ snapshot/persistence test compliant on 2 Jan 2023; grace to ~10 Jul 2023 once threshold met. Under all-employer 1 Jan 2023 disconnect reading, non-compliant for lacking policy on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees. Written disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute policy to new employees citing cost. Under 25+ snapshot test no statutory duty. Under all-employer electronic monitoring regime the employer monitors, has a written policy, but fails to provide it to new employees – distribution breach. Substantive existence is met, procedural distribution is disputed. Voluntary policy does not create statutory distribution obligation absent statutory duty to have policy.

C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has written and appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Current round consensus: D is the employer not in compliance as of 2 Jan 2023 because it was 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, thus in scope for electronic monitoring on the snapshot date, has never developed a required electronic monitoring policy, and the later fall to 24 does not extinguish the continuing duty. The group has converged in round 4 on the persistence-of-snapshot / continuing-obligation reading.
